From af (“off”) + bilde (“to form”), calque of German abbilden and Latin dēpingō.
Equivalent to af (“off”) + stand (“standing”), calque of German Abstand (“distance, interval”), which is in turn a calque of Latin distantia

Via German Antilope, from Medieval Latin antilops, from Byzantine Greek ἀνθόλοψ (anthólops).

parole.significato: Athenian, a citizen or resident of Athens (the capital city of Greece).
parole.testo: Via German Athenienser, from Latin Athēniēnsis, from Athēnae + -ēnsis.

parole.significato: Athenian, belonging to the Greek city of Athens.
parole.testo: Via German atheniensisch, from Latin Athēniēnsis, from Athēnae + -ēnsis.
Via German Atom n and Latin atomus f from Ancient Greek ἄτομοι (φύσεις) f (átomoi (phúseis)), ἄτομα (σώματα) n (átoma (sṓmata), “indivisible particles of matter”).

parole.significato: Attic, belonging to the landscape of Attica or the city of Athens
parole.testo: Via German attisch and Latin Atticus from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós).
From German Baronesse, from Medieval Latin baronissa.

parole.significato: beast (a cruel and violent being or creature)
parole.testo: From German Bestie, from Latin bēstia (“beast”).

parole.significato: a Brit, Briton (a person from Great Britain)
parole.testo: Borrowed via German Brite from Latin Brittō, Brittō (“Brit, Breton”).

From del (“part”) + tage (“take”). Partial calque of German teilnehmen, itself probably a calque of Latin participō (“to partake of, participate in”); compare corresponding calques such as Low German deelnehmen, deilnähmen, Dutch deelnemen, English take part, Icelandic taka þátt, Swedish delta and N

parole.significato: European (person living or originating from Europe, or sometimes only the European Union)
parole.testo: Via German Europäer and Latin Europaeus from Ancient Greek Εὐρωπαῖος (Eurōpaîos), from Εὐρώπη (Eurṓpē) + -αῖος (-aîos).
Via German europäisch and Latin Europaeus from Ancient Greek Εὐρωπαῖος (Eurōpaîos), from Εὐρώπη (Eurṓpē) + -αῖος (-aîos).

parole.significato: torch (a stick with a flame at one end)
parole.testo: Derived from German Fackel, from Latin facula, diminutive of fax (“torch”).

parole.significato: family (father, mother and their sons and daughters)
parole.testo: Borrowed via German Familie from Latin familia (“family, household”), derived from famulus (“servant, slave”). Displaced native Danish æt (“family, descent”).
From German Fase, from Latin facies.

From German Vorhaut, a calque of Latin praeputium.

Via German Physik and Latin physica from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ, “natural science”), a nominalization of the adjective φυσικός (phusikós, “natural”), derived from the noun φύσις (phúsis, “nature”). In the sense "physique", it is borrowed from French physique m.

Via German germanisch from Latin Germānus.
From German Gips, from Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos).

parole.significato: grammar (a system of rules and structures of a language, especially morphology and syntax)
parole.testo: Via German Grammatik and Latin grammatica from Ancient Greek γραμματική (grammatikḗ, “study of language and literature”). Derived from γράμματα n pl (grámmata, “alphabet, literature”).

parole.significato: grammarian (a person studying the grammar of a language or grammar in general)
parole.testo: Equivalent to grammatik (“grammar”) + -er. Via German Grammatiker and Latin grammaticus from Ancient Greek γραμματικός (grammatikós, “teacher of reading and literature”). Derived from γράμματα n pl (grámmata, “alphabet, literature”).
Via German historisch, from Latin historicus.
From German Intelligenz, from Latin intelligentia.

From German Jux, from Latin iocus.

From German Kachel, from Vulgar Latin *cacculus, a diminutive of caccabus (“cooking pot”), from Ancient Greek κάκκαβος (kákkabos).
From German Kappe, from Medieval Latin capa (“hooded cloak”). Doublet of kåbe.

Via German klassisch from Latin classicus (“of the (first) class”).

Borrowed via German Komödie and Latin cōmoedia from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία (kōmōidía, “comedy”), a derivation from κωμῳδός (kōmōidós, “performer of comedy”), a compound of κῶμος (kômos, “revel”) + ἀοιδός (aoidós, “singer”).
Borrowed via German komisch and Latin cōmicus from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós, “concerning comedy”), a derivation from κῶμος (kômos, “revel”).
From German Konfekt, from Medieval Latin confectum, perfect participle of Medieval Latin conficere.
From German Kongruenz, from Latin congruentia, from congruēns, the present active participle of congruere (“to unite, combine, agree”).

parole.significato: folder (physical object for storing sheets of paper)

Via German martern (“to torment”), derived from Marter (“torture”), from Late Latin martyrium (“martyrdom”) from Ancient Greek μαρτύριον (martúrion, “testimony”).
Borrowed via German Masse from Latin massa (“lump, bulk”), which is itself a loan from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “barley bread”).
From German Meierei, from Meier (“manager”) + -ei, from Medieval Latin maior (domūs) (“administrator”), from maior (“larger”), the comparative of magnus. Compare also English mayor.
From German Moll, from Latin mollis (“soft”).
Via German Mortalität, ultimately from Latin mortalitas.

From German Notiz (“note”), from Latin nōtitia (“fame, renown, celebrity”), from nōtus (“famous, well-known”).

parole.significato: mammal (an animal of the class Mammalia)

Via German Personale, from Latin personalis.
Via German personifizieren, from Latin persona + -ficere.
From German Poet, from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs).

Via German politisch and New Latin politicus from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós, “relating to the state”), derived from the noun πόλις (pólis, “city, state”).

parole.testo: Via German Spartaner and Latin Spartānus
Borrowed from German Spatel (“painting knife, spatula”), from Latin spatula, diminutive of Latin spatha (“spattle, shovel”).
From German Spektakel, from Latin spectaculum (“show”).
Via German Stativ n, from Latin statīvus (“stationary”).
Via German Syrer and Latin Syrus from Ancient Greek Σύρος (Súros).

parole.significato: talent (potential or factual ability to perform a skill better than most people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Talent (“talent”), from Latin talentum, from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance, a particular weight, especially of gold, sum of money, a talent”).
From German Tapete, from Latin tapete.
From German Theoretiker, from Latin theōrēticus, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).
Via German theoretisch, from Latin theoreticus, Derived from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).

Via German tragisch and Latin tragicus from Ancient Greek τραγικός (tragikós, “of or relating to tragedy”). Apparently a derivation from τράγος (trágos, “goat”).

parole.significato: trapezium (UK), trapezoid (US); quadrangle with two opposite sides parallel
parole.testo: Borrowed via German Trapez and Latin trapezium from Ancient Greek τραπέζιον (trapézion, “irregular quadrilateral”), diminutive of τράπεζα (trápeza, “table”).
A contraction of tunfisk, from German Thunfisch (“tuna”), from Latin thunnus, from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos).

parole.significato: to sign (to put one's name on a document to validate it)
parole.testo: From under (“under”) + skrive (“to write”). Calque of German unterschreiben and Latin subscrībō.
